question: How does a keyboard habit become an orchestral texture?
intro: Rapid semiquavers turn a pianist’s warm-up into orchestral conversation. Hew David Steuart-Powell’s portrait makes the strings behave like fingers running over a keyboard.

sections.label: II · The pianist’s warm-up
sections.mNote: short chromatic figures pass between the strings

cues.title: Strings imitate a keyboard
cues.text: Quick semiquaver figures pass between the violin parts. They suggest a toccata, but their chromatic notes make the supposed warm-up less predictable than a simple scale.
cues.evidence: Novello pp. 8–14; Elgar’s commentary identifies the pianist’s warm-up and chromatic toccata idea. This describes the whole short variation. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_Variations
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Hew David Steuart-Powell
cues.text: The pianist Hew David Steuart-Powell plays chamber music with Elgar on violin and Basil Nevinson on cello. His habit of running over the keys before playing supplies the joke in this portrait.
cues.evidence: The Elgar Society identifies the pianist and his chamber-music connection; Elgar’s commentary describes the preparatory runs. https://elgar.org/3enigma.htm https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_Variations

source.title: Elgar, Enigma Variations, full score (Novello)
source.locator: PDF pp. 8–14, rehearsal figures 5–7. Whole-variation passage map, using the report’s 0:12, 0:16 and 0:22 changes and the final decline. Timing is approximate; desks indicate activity within a span.

timeline.note: Semiquaver figures begin as an exchange between the two violin sections (p. 8).
Woodwind replies join the running string figures (pp. 8–9).
Fast figures and accented wind responses share the stronger middle span (pp. 10–11).
Wind fragments stand out as the strings alternate running figures with lighter accompaniment (p. 12).
The final string exchange has quiet wind responses and a marked solo-timpani figure (pp. 13–14).
Short flute and clarinet solos close the variation over sparse lower strings; the running violins stop (p. 14).

composer.epithet: A Worcester violinist who made orchestral variations into portraits of friends and the concerto into an argument with memory.
facts: Largely self-taught; violin, organ, orchestral playing and his father’s Worcester music shop
Bandmaster, Worcester County Asylum, Powick, 1879–84 · organist, St George’s Catholic Church, 1885–89 · Master of the King’s Musick, 1924–34
Two completed symphonies; violin and cello concertos; choral works; chamber music; five completed Pomp and Circumstance marches
composer.background:
Elgar learned the orchestra from inside it. His father William kept a music shop in Worcester, tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church. Edward read the scores in the shop, played violin in local ensembles, taught several instruments and eventually succeeded his father at the organ. He was born in Lower Broadheath in 1857, a Catholic in a predominantly Anglican musical establishment and a tradesman’s son in a profession increasingly organised around London colleges. He remained sensitive to both distinctions throughout his later success. His practical education taught him how a phrase feels under a bow.

At Powick he wrote quadrilles and polkas for an unusual ensemble, learning to give each instrument useful work. The Three Choirs Festival brought larger repertory within reach: Handel, Mendelssohn and contemporary oratorio, alongside orchestral music from the Continent. Visits to London widened that education. Wagner mattered particularly: the chromatic connection between chords, the orchestral recollection of earlier events and the long postponement of a cadence all entered Elgar’s language. His mature scores acquired part of their English character through their subsequent public use.
